lead: A mutex lock and a semaphore both stop two processes from entering the same critical section together. A mutex has one owner: only the process that acquired it may release it. A semaphore is an integer with two atomic operations, wait and signal, so it can guard a pool of identical resources and also enforce an order between processes. The kernel's queues, the row locks behind a UPI payment, and the seat counter at IRCTC all rest on these ideas.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for the critical section and race conditions, and 3.2 for atomic test-and-set and compare-and-swap.

sections.h3: Mutex lock: one owner at a time

blocks.text: A mutex is a shared flag locked with two operations. A process calls acquire() before its critical section and release() after it. acquire() tests and sets the flag in one atomic step using hardware instructions from 3.2, so two processes cannot both see it free.
The mutex gives mutual exclusion: at most one process holds the lock. It also gives ownership: only the acquirer may release it, and the OS records the owner.

If the lock is taken, acquire() may spin in a tight loop: a spinlock. Spinning burns CPU but avoids a context switch, so it suits a few instructions on a multicore machine. On one CPU, or for a long section, the waiter should sleep in a queue instead. POSIX threads provide the blocking form as pthread_mutex_lock and pthread_mutex_unlock.

sections.h3: Semaphore: an integer with atomic wait and signal

blocks.text: A semaphore S is an integer, a queue of waiting processes, and two atomic operations. Some syllabi call wait P (proberen, to test) and signal V (verhogen, to increase); others call them down and up.
wait(S): S = S − 1, then block the caller if S < 0.   signal(S): S = S + 1, then wake one waiter if S ≤ 0.
blocks.where: S is set once before any process runs. |S| is the number of blocked processes when S is negative. When S ≥ 0, S is the number of free permits.

blocks.text: The change to S and the test must run without interruption. If two processes decrement S together, both can read the same old value and one permit is lost. The kernel disables interrupts for these instructions, or uses a spinlock inside the semaphore code. A blocked waiter joins S's queue; signal removes one and makes it ready. FIFO order is common but not promised by the definition.

items: Binary semaphore: S is only 0 or 1. It acts like a mutex but has no owner, so any process may signal it.
Counting semaphore: S starts at N and guards N identical resources, such as N printers.

sections.h3: Two uses: mutual exclusion and ordering

blocks.text: Mutual exclusion. Set S = 1. Each process does wait(S) before the critical section and signal(S) after it. The first leaves S = 0 and enters; the second drops S to −1 and blocks; the first's signal raises S to 0 and wakes the second.

Ordering. Set S = 0. Process A runs A1, then signal(S). Process B does wait(S), then B1. B blocks until A finishes A1. This is condition synchronisation: the semaphore carries a signal, not a lock. Starting at 1 would let B run first.
Bounded buffer (producer–consumer). There are n slots and three semaphores: mutex = 1, empty = n, full = 0.

The counting semaphores count slots and items; mutex protects the buffer. Wait on empty or full before wait(mutex). A producer that takes mutex first and sleeps on empty holds the lock, so the consumer cannot enter and both hang.

Readers–writers. Many readers may read together; a writer needs the data alone. Use mutex = 1, rw_mutex = 1, read_count = 0. A reader does wait(mutex), read_count++, and if read_count == 1 also wait(rw_mutex); then signal(mutex). On exit: wait(mutex), read_count−−, and if read_count == 0 signal(rw_mutex); then signal(mutex). A writer does wait(rw_mutex) … signal(rw_mutex). Continuous readers can starve a writer.

Dining philosophers. Five philosophers, five chopsticks, each a semaphore at 1. Philosopher i does wait(chopstick[i]), wait(chopstick[(i + 1) mod 5]), eats, signals both. If all five take the left chopstick, each waits forever for the right: circular wait, a deadlock (see 3.5). Fixes: allow at most four to pick up at once (counting semaphore at 4); let odd-numbered philosophers pick the right chopstick first; or use one mutex so only one picks at a time.

figure.caption: The worked example with S = 1: each row gives S, the blocked set, and who runs. S falls to 0, −1 and −2; the negative values count the blocked processes, and the final signal raises S to −1 and wakes P2, so P2 enters while P3 stays blocked.

spec.title: S, blocked, who runs
spec.aria: A five-row table of the worked example: S starts at 1; P1's wait leaves S = 0 and P1 runs; P2's wait makes S = −1 and blocks P2; P3's wait makes S = −2 and blocks P3; P1's signal raises S to −1 and wakes P2, leaving P3 blocked.

examples.question: A counting semaphore S is initialised to 1. Processes P1, P2 and P3 call wait(S) in that order, with no signal in between. (a) Give S and the set of blocked processes after each call. (b) P1 then calls signal(S). Give S and state who can enter the critical section. (6 marks)
steps: P1 calls wait(S): S = 1 − 1 = 0. Is 0 < 0? No, so P1 continues and enters the critical section. S = 0, blocked = {}.
P2 calls wait(S): S = 0 − 1 = −1. Is −1 < 0? Yes, so P2 blocks. S = −1, blocked = {P2}. |S| = 1 waiter.
P3 calls wait(S): S = −1 − 1 = −2. Is −2 < 0? Yes, so P3 blocks. S = −2, blocked = {P2, P3}. |S| = 2 waiters.
P1 calls signal(S): S = −2 + 1 = −1. Is −1 ≤ 0? Yes, so one waiter wakes; FIFO wakes P2. S = −1, blocked = {P3}.
P1 has left the critical section, so P2 enters. P3 stays blocked until P2 signals.
examples.answer: S is 0, −1, −2 after the three waits, with blocked sets {}, {P2} and {P2, P3}; the signal sets S = −1 and wakes P2, so P2 enters and P3 remains blocked (6 marks).
examples.check:
S = 1
blocked = []
for p in ['P1', 'P2', 'P3']:
    S -= 1
    if S < 0:
        blocked.append(p)
    print(S)
S += 1
if S <= 0:
    blocked.pop(0)
print(S)

traps: wait tests S < 0; signal tests S ≤ 0. Mixing them loses a wake-up or wakes a process with no permit.
A negative S counts blocked processes, not free resources. S = −2 means two waiters, not two resources free.
An ordering semaphore starts at 0; a mutex semaphore starts at 1. Starting the ordering one at 1 lets the second process run first.
A mutex must be released by its owner; any process may signal a semaphore, so a stray signal breaks the count.
In the bounded buffer, wait(mutex) must come after wait(empty) or wait(full). Reversing them is the examiner's favourite deadlock question.

quiz.q: Define a binary semaphore and give its two allowed values.
quiz.a: A semaphore restricted to 0 and 1. wait lowers it and blocks if it goes below 0; signal raises it and wakes a waiter if it is 0 or below.

quiz.q: Why does a semaphore used for ordering start at 0 rather than 1?
quiz.a: At 0, the second process's first wait(S) makes S = −1 and blocks it until the first process signals. At 1, the second process would pass immediately and the order would be lost.

quiz.q: Why must wait and signal be atomic?
quiz.a: Each changes S and then tests it. Two processes changing S together can read the same old value, so a permit is lost or a waiter is never woken. Atomicity makes each operation one indivisible step.

quiz.q: A counting semaphore S = 3 guards three printers. Four processes call wait(S) in order, with no signal between. Give S after each call and say how many block.
quiz.a: S becomes 2, 1, 0, −1. The first three processes get printers; the fourth blocks, and |S| = 1 confirms one waiter.

quiz.q: A bounded buffer has n = 4 slots and currently holds 2 items. Give the values of empty, full and mutex.
quiz.a: empty = 4 − 2 = 2 free slots, full = 2 items present, mutex = 1 because no process is inside the buffer code.

quiz.q: A producer does wait(mutex) before wait(empty) in the bounded buffer. Explain how this can deadlock.
quiz.a: The buffer is full; the producer holds mutex and blocks on empty. The consumer cannot enter because mutex is held, so it can never remove an item and never signals empty. Producer waits for empty, consumer waits for mutex: a cycle, so both hang.

quiz.q: In the dining philosophers with five semaphore chopsticks started at 1, explain how deadlock forms and give one fix that removes circular wait.
quiz.a: Each philosopher takes the left chopstick and then waits for the right one, held by the neighbour on the right. All five hold one chopstick and wait forever: circular wait plus hold and wait. Fix: the odd-numbered philosopher picks the right chopstick first, so no cycle of holders and waiters can close.

beyond: Not for the exam. Linux builds mutexes on futexes: spin briefly in user space, then sleep in the kernel on contention. Blocking locks bring priority inversion, where a low-priority holder delays a high-priority waiter; priority inheritance is the usual cure. Named semaphores still coordinate unrelated processes, and counting semaphores reappear as permits in thread pools and connection limits.
